passage: Before I said a word to my parents, Dilnaz and I sat at the kitchen table with a notepad. We had been pulled two ways all year, and every holiday was a small negotiation. So we wrote down what we both wanted: one long trip to my parents each year, one to Dilnaz's, and a quiet holiday at home every other year. We disagreed about how long each trip should be, argued a little, and settled on five days. Only then did I phone my parents. I said, "Dilnaz and I have decided together how we'd like to plan visits," and read out the list. There was a long pause, and my father said he wished we had told them sooner. It was not a happy call, but nobody could say Dilnaz was behind it. We had one voice. - Ujjwal

passage:
Family therapist's note — Divyansh and Radhika, session four. Written by Thomas.

For three months, Divyansh's parents had expected the couple every weekend and for every holiday. Each time Radhika raised it, Divyansh either went quiet or promised to "talk to them", and each time his parents heard it as Radhika's idea.
In today's session I asked them what they wanted before deciding who would speak. They talked for twenty minutes. They agreed: one weekend a month with his parents, Diwali with his side, Christmas with hers, and one short trip alone each year.
Divyansh said he would call his parents on Sunday. Radhika asked to be on the call, but not to speak first.
Follow-up, one week later: Divyansh told his parents, "We've decided together." His mother was unhappy but did not blame Radhika this time.
What I did next: we will look at how the first month goes.

qa.q: Which festival did the couple agree to spend with Radhika's side?
How might Radhika have felt before the couple agreed a shared position?
qa.a: Radhika likely felt frustrated and alone, since his parents heard every request as Radhika's idea.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh and Radhika do if his parents push back later?
qa.a: They could repeat the same shared decision calmly together, and maybe suggest trying it for a few months before judging it.

qa.q: How does the couple's approach look to Divyansh's mother?
qa.a: His mother is unhappy about fewer visits, but hearing it as a joint decision from her son stops her from blaming Radhika.

grounding: It shows a couple deciding their shared position on visits and holidays first, then the husband talking to his parents so they see a united couple.

passage:
Saturday, late

Anusha and I finally did it the right way round.
Every time my parents asked why we weren't coming to Nashik for the long weekend, I'd mumble, then Anusha would say something, and Mummy would decide it was her fault. My brother Madhav even joked that Anusha "controls the calendar".
So tonight, before calling anyone, we sat down and decided together. Two long weekends a year in Nashik. Diwali alternating between both families. Christmas with just us, because it's the only holiday we both get off.
Then I called Mummy and Papa myself. I said, "We've talked, and this is what we've decided." Not "Anusha wants". We.
Mummy was quiet, then asked about Diwali. Papa said, "If it's both of you, fine."
Madhav texted later: "Heard you did the grown-up thing." I'll take it.
— Vishal

qa.q: How many long weekends a year did Vishal and Anusha plan in Nashik?
How did Vishal seem to feel after Madhav's text?
qa.a: Vishal seemed pleased and quietly proud, glad the call went better than the old mumbling.

qa.q: What else could Vishal and Anusha do if a family emergency changed the plan?
qa.a: They could talk together first and then tell both families a joint decision, the same way, so the plan bends without blame.

qa.q: How might Anusha see Vishal making the call directly?
qa.a: Anusha likely feels supported and relieved, since the plan is presented as "we" and she's no longer blamed as the one controlling the calendar.

grounding: It shows a couple deciding their shared position on visits first and the husband then telling his parents, so the family sees a united couple.
